questions.q: What is the standard unit used to measure the volume of a box that has dimensions in centimetres?
questions.a: The unit is cubic centimetres (cm³). If a student says "cm" or "sq cm," they are confusing volume with length or area, indicating they have not yet distinguished between 1D, 2D, and 3D measurements.

questions.q: If you have a cube with a side length of 2 cm, why is its volume 8 cm³ and not 6 cm³?
questions.a: The volume is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³, because you are multiplying the length, width, and height (all of which are 2 cm). A student saying 6 cm³ is likely adding the sides (2+2+2) or multiplying by 3, which ignores the 3D nature of the object.

questions.q: A shipping box is 5 m long, 2 m wide, and 3 m high. Calculate its volume.
questions.a: Volume = 5 m × 2 m × 3 m = 30 m³. A student who gets a different answer likely added the numbers (10) or missed one dimension, showing a struggle with the multiplication rule for 3D space.

questions.q: If you double the length, width, and height of a cube, does the volume also double? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: No, the volume increases by 8 times (2 × 2 × 2 = 8). A student who says "double" is applying linear thinking to 3D volume, failing to realize that changing all three dimensions compounds the effect.

questions.q: Is it possible for two different-looking cuboids to have the same volume? Provide an example.
questions.a: Yes. A cuboid of 4 × 3 × 2 cm (volume 24 cm³) and a cuboid of 6 × 2 × 2 cm (volume 24 cm³) have the same volume. If a student says no, they believe volume is tied to the shape's specific "look" rather than the total capacity.

questions.q: Design a box that has a volume of 36 cm³. What could be its possible dimensions?
questions.a: Any three numbers that multiply to 36 (e.g., 6 × 3 × 2, or 9 × 2 × 2, or 4 × 3 × 3). A poor answer would be a single number (like 36) or an incorrect set of factors, indicating a lack of understanding of the volume formula.
